texts.full_text: erebellar Cyst with Pseudomeningocele After Tumor Removal at the Craniovertebral Junction. Cerebellar cyst formation after surgery is uncommon, and few cases of this condition have been previously reported. These cases had an intraparenchymal cyst in the cerebellar hemisphere that required surgical fenestration of the cyst. We herein present a rare case of a postoperative cerebellar cyst with pseudomeningocele and magnetic resonance images indicating a fistula between the cyst and pseudomeningocele. A patient presented wiA patient presented with symptoms such as gait instability, dysmetria, and nystagmus a few weeks after undergoing a tumor removal surgery at the craniovertebral junction. The initial assessment included a neurological examination, which revealed signs of cerebellar dysfunction. Subsequent imaging studies, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), showed an expansive lesion in the cerebellum with a high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and gadolinium enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted images. The lesion was associated with a nearby pseudomeningocele, which is a cystic sac filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and lined by CSF-derived cells. The unique feature of this case was the identification of a communication between the cerebellar cyst and the pseudomeningocele on MRI using susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI) technique. This connection appeared as a linear structure with signal void, suggesting a fistula between the cyst and the pseudomeningocele. The presence of this fistula was likely responsible for the delayed presentation of the patient's symptoms postoperatively. The treatment plan involved a multidisciplinary approach, combining neurosurgery and radiotherapy. Surgical intervention consisted of resection of the cerebellar cyst to prevent further CSF leakage into the pseudomeningocele, as well as duraplasty to reinforce the dural defect. Additionally, given the proximity and potential communication with the tumor site, prophylactic stereotactic radiosurgery was considered to minimize the risk

For analysis purposes, the following notations are introduced:CC: Computation cost;$T_{h}$: CC of single hash function;$T_{se}$: CC of symmetric encryption/decryption. [Table 5](#sensors-19-04752-t005){ref-type="table"} shows the computation cost analysis. The protocol presented in \[[@B23-sensors-19-04752]\] incurs $2T_{h}$, $3T_{h}$, and $5T_{h}$, for each tag, Reader and Server, respectively, making its total computation cost $10T_{h}$. Similarly, the computation cost of protocol presented in \[[@B30-sensors-19-04752]\] is $2T_{h}$, $2T_{h}$, and $3T_{h}$, respectively, for each participant, totaling it to $7T_{h}$. The protocol presented in \[[@B21-sensors-19-04752]\] requires $4T_{h}$, $2T_{h}$, and $6T_{h}$ for each tag, Reader, and Server, respectively, totaling it to $12T_{h}$. The computation cost of the protocol of Gope and Hwang \[[@B3-sensors-19-04752]\] is $5T_{h}$, $2T_{h}$, and $7T_{h}$, respectively, for each participant totaling it to $14T_{h}$. In comparison, the tag in proposed protocol uses $2T_{h}$, the Reader uses $2T_{h}$, and the Server requires $4T_{h} + 2T_{se}$, so in total the computation cost of the proposed protocol is equal to $8T_{h} + 2T_{se}$. Considering the experiment of Kilinc and Yanik \[[@B47-sensors-19-04752]\], the computation time of $T_{h}$ is 0.0023 ms, whereas the computation time to calculate $T_{se}$ is 0.0046 ms. The experiment was performed on a Ubuntu system with an Intel dual-core Pentium processor with specifications, including 2.20 GHz, 2048 MB processor and Ram, respectively.
